scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that most students benefit from study abroad while arguing 'all' is too strong; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Time spent living in another country can change how a young person sees the world.
Some people argue that all college and university students would benefit from spending at least one semester studying abroad.
I agree that most students would gain a great deal, but I do not believe the word all is true for everyone.
First, the great majority of students would indeed benefit from studying abroad.
Living in a new culture teaches lessons about language, customs, and independence that no classroom can.
For example, a student who studies overseas often returns more confident, mature, and open-minded.
This shows that time abroad can shape a young person in valuable and lasting ways.
Students abroad also build friendships and skills that serve them in a connected world.
Facing an unfamiliar place forces young people to solve problems and grow on their own.
For most students, then, a semester abroad is genuinely worthwhile.
Second, however, the claim that all students would benefit goes too far.
Some students have health conditions or family duties that make studying abroad very difficult.
Consider a student caring for a sick parent, for whom a semester overseas would bring more harm than good.
Such cases show that the same experience is not equally good for everyone.
A student in deep financial trouble might gain little from an experience that leaves her in debt.
For a few, the stress and cost of going abroad could outweigh any benefit.
Studying abroad, then, helps most students but not absolutely all of them.
In conclusion, the great majority of students would benefit from a semester abroad.
But the word all is too strong, since some students face real barriers or needs.
The wiser claim is that most students gain from studying abroad and should be encouraged to do so.
